findings.passage: Dakota Johnson has a reputation, as Vogue put it in its October 2026 cover story, for "a certain cool-girl deadpan opacity, a kind of mischievous remove during press appearances." She earned it.
findings.problem: Orientation. The opening three paragraphs and the 60-word type answer never say who Johnson is. A reader without prior knowledge only infers she is an actress from "a bold actress" in the type section. They learn why she is famous (Fifty Shades) in the fourth section, about 800 words in. Her parents, Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith, are named without a descriptor, while Tippi Hedren gets one. The reason people are searching now (the Vogue cover and Verity) appears only in the last section.
findings.acceptance_test: Before the type H2, one sourced clause or sentence tells a cold reader that Johnson is an American actress and producer best known for the Fifty Shades of Grey films. The limes hook stays first. Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith get a one- or two-word descriptor (e.g., actors) on first mention.

findings.passage: If authenticity is the creed, the put-ons need explaining, and they predate the current persona.
findings.problem: The Ellen exchange is filed as one of the "put-ons," but the clip (S09) shows Johnson telling the truth: DeGeneres concedes, "I think I do remember I was invited." The evidence record's own inference (C09) is that she refused to absorb a false story about herself. A reader new to the clip will think the correction was another prank. That muddles the section's bit-versus-faked-feeling argument and risks misrepresenting a widely known moment. Nothing tells the reader why the clip is famous, so "It will haunt me" has no stakes.
findings.acceptance_test: The Ellen exchange is no longer presented as an example of a put-on. The prose makes plain that Johnson's line was true and that DeGeneres conceded. If it stays in this section, it is used explicitly as the contrast: she refused to go along with a false story even when it was played as a joke. One sourced clause (e.g., S17) says why the clip became famous, so "It will haunt me" lands.

findings.passage: On set, she said, "We'd do the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then we would do the takes of the movie that we wanted to make," and she rewrote scenes the night before.
findings.problem: Two quotations refer to "Erika," but the article only ever calls the author E.L. James and never says that Erika is her first name. A reader new to the story meets an apparently new person at the paragraph's most important quote.
findings.acceptance_test: Before or at the first "Erika" quotation, the text says that Erika is E.L. James's first name (or a bracketed [James] is used where the quote allows it). The two later "Erika" quotes then read without ambiguity.

findings.passage: Shortly after _Madame Web_ opened in February 2024, she told Bustle she "probably will never do anything like it again because I don't make sense in that world."
findings.problem: Madame Web is never identified. A reader who doesn't know it was a superhero franchise film can't tell what "that world" means or why the contrast with her own company matters. The same gap affects The Ringer's opening-day piece and the Nine paragraph's "along for the ride." Madame Web is also a meta keyword, so searchers will arrive expecting context.
findings.acceptance_test: On first mention, a sourced descriptor identifies Madame Web's genre (and its reception, if a source supports it), so "that world" is legible without outside knowledge. No unsourced box-office or review claims are added.

findings.passage: In a bleak political moment, "if I didn't try and apply great meaning to little things, I honestly don't think I'd make it."
findings.problem: "A bleak political moment" is vague enough to puzzle any reader. The Vanity Fair source (S02) shows she was speaking about reading that Roe v. Wade was likely to be overturned, in 2022. Hiding the context makes the quote float and weakens the meaning-over-reassurance point it supports.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence either names the context the Vanity Fair source gives, with its 2022 date, or drops the framing and attributes the quote plainly. No unexplained "political moment" remains.

findings.passage: That sits at least as close to a Three as to a Four.
findings.problem: Type Three is raised twice as a fit for her behavior: here, and in "a control-minded Eight or a strategic Three". But the type answer, the FAQ and the section headings list only Six, Eight, Nine and Seven as rivals. A reader can't tell whether Three is a live hypothesis the article forgot to test or just a passing comparison. The metadata and body disagree.
findings.acceptance_test: Either Three gets a short test in the alternatives (why "this is a business" and her press savvy don't make image or success her core motive) and appears consistently in the answer/FAQ list of rivals, or both mentions are reworded so they don't read as an untested fifth hypothesis. Body, the 60-word answer and the FAQ name the same set of alternatives.

findings.passage: The put-ons are the biggest loose end. The line between a bit and a faked feeling is this profile's inference, and her limes confession changed within a single year.
findings.problem: Momentum. The body is 3,918 words, above the 2,000–3,500 target. Four consecutive typology sections (Type 6, safety, Eight/Nine/Seven, what's left open; about 1,400 words) let the person recede. Some of that is restatement: this sentence repeats the end of "The bit and the feeling" ("That is an inference from her words, not a rule she has stated, and the limes show it has fuzzy edges"). The source-limit caveat about Taylor-Johnson and The Ringer partly repeats the earlier "flattering profiles" caveat.
findings.acceptance_test: The "leaves open" section adds only items not already stated as limits earlier, with no second statement of the bit/feeling inference caveat. The body is at most 3,500 words. No protected passage is cut, and no evidence from the Type 6 case or the safety discriminator is lost.

findings.passage: Foley's remark matters most because it predates the candid persona.
findings.problem: "The candid persona" (and "the current persona" earlier in the section) is never defined or dated. A cold reader can't tell whether it means the press-prankster reputation or the later "authentic" vocabulary, or when either began. The Foley remark and the Dornan put-on both come from the same 2017 Vogue piece, so the dating argument can't be followed as written.
findings.acceptance_test: One dated, sourced sentence says which persona is meant and roughly when it became her public reputation, so a reader can check that Foley's 2017 remark comes before it. Otherwise the sentence is reworded to make a claim the dates support.

protected_passages.passage: Not that she was good, or that she had arrived. That she did something different.
protected_passages.reason: Turns a career anecdote into the article's first real insight in two short sentences. A cold reader learns what she values before any typology appears.

protected_passages.passage: She didn't say lying was hard. She said faking it was, in the same breath as finding it hard "to go along with the silliness of doing a press tour."
protected_passages.reason: This close reading resolves the title's paradox from her own words, and it is honest about being an inference. It is the hinge that makes the prankster and the authenticity claims readable as one person.

protected_passages.passage: What separates the readings is what safety does for her. For a Six, security is usually the goal. Johnson almost always describes it as the condition for something else.
protected_passages.reason: States the discriminator in plain language that needs no Enneagram background, and it pays off the 'what is the safety for?' question set up in the type section.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven's appetite usually runs from that sentence. Hers runs toward it.
protected_passages.reason: Tests a rival type against her own quote in eight words. Distinctive, memorable, and specific to her.

protected_passages.passage: For most actors, wrap is the end of a job. For Johnson it means losing, again, the kind of set Vogue says she joined the industry for: "a safe container full of artists feeling free."
protected_passages.reason: The ending lands on a concrete, sourced, unusual detail rather than a thesis restatement, and it ties safety, feeling and the work together.

assessment: For a cold reader, this is an engaging, well-paced profile. The limes-and-Vogue opening creates a real puzzle: a prankster who says she can't fake it. The two questions in the type section give the reader a map, and the safety discriminator pays it off clearly. Vivid, specific details carry the middle: the teacher reading a tabloid, Fincher's 'something different', the Erika takes, the deferred fees, the Easter Bunny, summer camp. The reader learns who she is through choices, not adjectives. The article is also unusually honest about self-report, promotional settings and the strength of the Six case. The main gaps are orientation and clarity. The reader isn't told she is an actress or why she is famous until about 800 words in. The Ellen correction is misfiled as a put-on when it was true. Several references assume prior knowledge: Erika, Madame Web, the 'bleak political moment', the 'candid persona'. Three is raised but never tested, and the piece runs about 400 words over target, with some repeated caveats in the typology run. Similarity advisory: not tripped. The maximum is 0.016 against a 0.04 threshold, inside the noise floor. Only 2 target units were parsed, so the advisory's coverage is thin. Its matches are generic type vocabulary with no shared phrases. Read directly, the arguments and details are specific to Johnson, so there is no reuse finding. Risk flags: sensitive allegations (her account of creative-control fights with a named living author, her parents' addiction, her depression) and contested typing (a live counterphobic Six rival at medium confidence) both remain true and warrant the expanded jury.
